--- license: apache-2.0 pipeline_tag: feature-extraction tags: - embedding - feature-extraction - sentence-transformers - multimodal-embedding - multimodal - vision - audio - video - image-feature-extraction - audio-feature-extraction - video-feature-extraction - sentence-similarity language: - multilingual library_name: transformers ---

Hugging Face | GitHub | Launch Blog | Documentation |
License: Apache 2.0 | Authors: Google DeepMind

**EmbeddingGemma 2** is an open multimodal embedding model built by Google DeepMind which maps text (incl. code), images, video, and audio inputs—and combinations thereof—into a single, unified 768-dimensional vector space. The model has 740M total parameters, combining a 270M parameter text model with modular vision (170M) and audio (300M) encoders. Designed to run on consumer hardware such as mobile devices and laptops, EmbeddingGemma 2 delivers low-latency semantic representations for on-device applications, like search, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), classification, and clustering. EmbeddingGemma 2 builds upon the architectural and capability advancements of Gemma 4, offering several core features:  * **Native multimodality:** Native multimodality: Unifies 4 modalities (text, images, video, and audio) in a single shared 768-dimensional embedding space. * **Multilinguality and code:** EmbeddingGemma 2 understands 100+ languages, and achieves a \~14% improvement on code tasks relative to its predecessor.  * **Flexible footprint:** Combines a 270M parameter text backbone (130M transformer \+ 140M embedder) with selectively loadable vision (170M) and audio (300M) encoders, allowing developers to load only the modalities required for their use case. * **Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL):** Native support for truncated embeddings across 128d, 256d, 512d, and 768d, enabling up to a **6x reduction** in vector storage costs with minimal impact on quality. * **Context length:** 8K token context window, capable of processing minutes of audio or video. * **Task-steered representations:** Uses lightweight text instruction prefixes to optimize embeddings for different tasks (search, classification, clustering, semantic similarity, etc.). ### Model Overview | Parameters | Total | 740M | | :---- | :---- | :---- | | | **Backbone** | 130M | | | **Embedder** | 140M | | | **Modality Encoders** | *Vision:* 170M *Audio:* 300M | | **Architecture** | **Layers** | 24 | | | **Model Dimension** | 512 | | | **Hidden Dimension** | 2048 | | | **Sliding Window** | 1024 tokens | | | **Vocabulary Size** | 262,144 | | | **\# Heads** | 4 | | | **\# KV-Heads (Local/Global)** | 2/1 | | | **Local:Global** | 5:1 | | | **Attention** | GQA/MQA | | | **Activation** | Gated FFN with GELU | | | **Pooling** | Mean Pooling | | | **Projection Layer** | 512→768 | | **Input/Output** | **Supported Modalities** | Text, Images, Video, Audio | | | **Context Window** | 8,192 tokens | | | **Native Output Dimension** | 768 | | | **MRL Truncation Dimensions** | 128, 256, 512 | ## **Benchmark Results** EmbeddingGemma 2 was evaluated across text, code, vision, visual document, video, and audio embedding benchmarks. All results reported below use the full-precision checkpoint. ### Overall Evaluation Results (768d) | Modality | Benchmark | Metric | EmbeddingGemma 2 | EmbeddingGemma 1 | | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | | *Text* | Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB, multilingual, v2) | Mean(Task), Multiple | 61.36 | 61.15 | | | Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB, code, v1) | Mean(Task), NDCG@10 | 78.68 | 68.76 | | *Image* | Massive Image Embedding Benchmark (MIEB, lite) | Mean(TaskType), Multiple | 64.64 | \- | | | Massive Multimodal Embedding Benchmark (MMEB v2 \- Image) | Mean(Task), Hit@1 | 57.28 | \- | | | Massive Multimodal Embedding Benchmark (MMEB v2 \- VisDoc) | Mean(Task), NDCG@5 | 67.84 | \- | | *Video* | Massive Multimodal Embedding Benchmark (MMEB v2 \- Video) | Mean(Task), Hit@1 | 50.67 | \- | | *Audio* | Massive Sound Embedding Benchmark (MSEB, Retrieval) | Mean(Task), MRR@10 | 69.54 | \- | | | Massive Audio Embedding Benchmark (MAEB) *Hugging Face*  | Mean(Task), Multiple | 49.39 | \- | ### Evaluation Results with Vector Truncation With MRL, EmbeddingGemma 2 representations can be truncated below the native 768d to 128d, 256d, and 512d representations and re-normalized. With this, model users can reduce storage requirements, with minimal quality impact down to 256d. 128d is best suited to text-only workloads. | Output Dimension | Compression Ratio | MTEB *(multilingual, v2) Mean(Task)* | MTEB *(eng, v2) Mean(Task)* | MTEB *(code, v1) Mean(Task)* | MIEB *(lite) Mean(TaskType)* | MMEB (v2) *Overall* | MSEB *(Retrieval) Mean(Task)* | MAEB *Mean(Task)* | | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | | 768d (Full) | 1:1 | 61.36 | 68.46 | 78.68 | 64.64 | 59.01 | 69.54 | 49.39 | | 512d | 1:1.5 | 61.17 | 68.41 | 77.24 | 64.32 | 58.38 | 69.18 | 49.21 | | 256d | 1:3 | 60.41 | 67.78 | 76.18 | 63.13 | 56.24 | 66.76 | 48.91 | | 128d | 1:6 | 57.89 | 65.68 | 71.41 | 59.06 | 45.65 | 56.71 | 46.92 | ## **Quick Start** Install the `sentence-transformers` library: ```bash pip install -U sentence-transformers transformers ``` Generate text embeddings: ```python

models.readme_content: --- license: apache-2.0 base_model: google/gemma-4-12B base_model_relation: finetune language: - en - zh pipeline_tag: text-generation library_name: gguf tags: - humanizer - transformers - safetensors - text-rewriting - rewriting - paraphrase - style-transfer - gguf - llama.cpp - gemma4 --- # humanizer **A 12B model that rewrites AI-written drafts (emails, essays, reports, forum posts; English and Chinese) so they read like a person wrote them.** It is trained to keep every number, unit, date, name and quote and to add nothing, and it runs locally. **Quick start:** get the app for **[Mac (Apple silicon)](https://github.com/sgaofen/humanizer-local-model/releases/download/app-v0.3.2/Humanizer-0.3.2-macos-arm64.dmg)** or **[Windows](https://github.com/sgaofen/humanizer-local-model/releases/download/app-v0.3.2/Humanizer-0.3.2-windows-x64-setup.exe)**, open it and paste a draft; it works offline. Without the app: [llama.cpp and other runtimes](#usage-without-the-app), or [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) for coding agents. ## Before and after Drafts from the held-out evaluation set. For each we generated 8 samples with the Q8_0 file (llama.cpp, the app's settings) and picked the one that reads best among those the fact judge passed; it is shown unedited, and all 8 samples are [on GitHub](https://github.com/sgaofen/humanizer-local-model/blob/main/eval/outputs/examples-12b-Q8_0_x8.json). These are picks: across the whole set the judge flagged 44 of the 420 English rewrites, 135 problems in all, 125 of them a single word or phrase. Read the result before you send it, especially numbers, dates and names. Results over the whole set are below. More examples (a forum answer, a Zhihu answer) are in the [GitHub README](https://github.com/sgaofen/humanizer-local-model#before-and-after). ## Results **95% judged human by Originality.ai** at its strictest setting (210 English drafts, bf16 weights, 2026-10-02): 11 of 210 rewrites were flagged as AI, against 26 for the previous release, and no AI detector was used anywhere in training. **376 of 420 English rewrites came back with no factual problem** from a strict LLM judge, measured on the `humanizer-12b-Q8_0.gguf` file you download; where it did find one, more than 9 in 10 fixes are a single word or phrase. Method, every genre and the Chinese results: [Evaluation details](#evaluation-details). ## Quantization: smaller files, closer to the full model Most GGUF files come from one `llama-quantize` pass that rounds every weight to the target type; our 2-bit, Q3 and Q4_K_M files go further. In the 2-bit and Q3 files, we measured how much each weight tensor hurts the model when it is squeezed and gave the sensitive tensors more bits and the robust ones fewer. All three were then trained layer by layer to reproduce the full model (quantization-aware training) and distilled from the full bf16 model, used as the teacher, on English and Chinese rewriting data. For the 2-bit file, a standard build of the same size picks the same next token as bf16 70% of the time; these steps take it to 81%, 85% and then 87%. The result is still an ordinary GGUF that any recent llama.cpp runs; Q6_K and Q8_0 are standard builds, because at those sizes there is almost nothing left to recover. Numbers behind every point, KL, per-file fact checks and how each file was made: [docs/QUANTIZATION.md](https://github.com/sgaofen/humanizer-local-model/blob/main/docs/QUANTIZATION.md). All GGUF files also have their own repo: [jialinyyzz/humanizer-GGUF](https://huggingface.co/jialinyyzz/humanizer-GGUF). **[Usage without the app](USAGE.md)** · [不用 App 怎么用](USAGE.zh.md) · [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) · [GitHub](https://github.com/sgaofen/humanizer-local-model) · [GGUF files](https://huggingface.co/jialinyyzz/humanizer-GGUF) · [Install guide](https://github.com/sgaofen/humanizer-local-model/blob/main/docs/INSTALL.md) · [中文说明](https://github.com/sgaofen/humanizer-local-model/blob/main/README.zh.md) > **Setting this up with an AI agent?** Point it at [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md): exact files, server command, prompt byte for byte, and a self-test. ## Quick start **App:** download the `.dmg` (Mac with Apple silicon) or the Windows installer from [Releases](https://github.com/sgaofen/humanizer-local-model/releases/latest) (current: [app 0.3.2](https://github.com/sgaofen/humanizer-local-model/releases/tag/app-v0.3.2), which can import `.docx` and PDF files and keeps any passage you mark with **Create fact** word for word). On first run it suggests one of five sizes for your memory (Q8_0, Q6_K, Q4_K_M, Q3 or 2-bit, down to 8 GB machines; app 0.3.0 and later) and downloads it once; after that it works offline. Sizes and quality notes: [Files](#files). **Command line, for long documents and agents:** `pipx install git+https://github.com/sgaofen/humanizer-local-model`, then `hz paper.md -o paper.out.md` (also `.txt` and `.docx`). --- license: apache-2.0 pipeline_tag: image-text-to-text tags: - minicpm-v - multimodal - On-Device Model - lightweight - moe library_name: transformers --- # MiniCPM-V 4.7 [GitHub](https://github.com/openbmb/MiniCPM-V) · [On-device results](#on-device-capability-and-efficiency) · [Evaluation](#evaluation) · [Examples](#examples) · [Usage](#usages) · [Model weights](#model-weights) · [DSpark](https://huggingface.co/openbmb/MiniCPM-V-4.7-35B-A3B-DSpark) **MiniCPM-V 4.7** is the latest model in the MiniCPM-V series, available in a **35B-A3B** variant, with **35B-A3B being the first MoE model in the MiniCPM-V series**. It builds on the family's single-image, multi-image, and video understanding capabilities, combining stronger foundation capabilities with efficient visual encoding and on-device inference. Notable features of MiniCPM-V 4.7 include: - 📱 **The First Open-Source MoE Model with Lossless, Smooth On-Device Inference.** With our [**Lookahead Expert Scheduling (LES)**](https://github.com/OpenBMB/llama.cpp-omni) technique introduced alongside MiniCPM-V 4.7, combined with fine-grained layer-wise quantization and DSpark speculative sampling integration, MiniCPM-V 4.7 35B-A3B becomes the **first open-source MoE model to run smoothly on-device without compromising performance**, achieving a decoding speed of **13+ tokens/s with just 3 GB of memory on iPhone 17 Pro Max**. - 🔥 **A New Pareto Frontier in Performance and Efficiency.** As model capabilities continue to advance, inference efficiency has become an important measure of a model's value. On resource-constrained devices, delivering the strongest possible capabilities within a limited resource budget calls for higher capability density. The **35B-A3B** variant of MiniCPM-V 4.7 advances the performance–efficiency Pareto frontier for MLLMs. In Instruct mode, 35B-A3B **achieves a higher overall score in less inference time than Qwen3.6 35B-A3B**. - 🚀 **Efficient Architecture.** Based on the intra-ViT early compression technique from [LLaVA-UHD v4](https://github.com/THUMAI-Lab/LLaVA-UHD-v4), MiniCPM-V 4.7 compresses visual tokens early within the vision encoder, reducing computation in subsequent encoder layers. It also supports **mixed 4x/16x visual token compression**, allowing developers to balance visual detail and inference cost across tasks. - 💻 **Broad Platform and Chip Support.** MiniCPM-V 4.7 supports **iOS, Android, and HarmonyOS**, together with open-source on-device deployment support. It also provides **day-0 support for chip platforms from Rockchip, Houmo, Intel, AMD, and Arm**, extending deployment options across mobile and local computing devices. - 🛠️ **Developer Friendly.** MiniCPM-V 4.7 supports [inference frameworks](https://github.com/OpenBMB/MiniCPM-o/blob/main/docs/deployment_en.md#supported-inference-and-training-frameworks-and-api) including SGLang, vLLM, llama.cpp, and Ollama, along with [fine-tuning frameworks](https://github.com/OpenBMB/MiniCPM-o/blob/main/docs/deployment_en.md#supported-inference-and-training-frameworks-and-api) including SWIFT and LLaMA-Factory. It provides GGUF, BNB, AWQ, and GPTQ quantized variants and adds **FP8 quantization support**. We also release [**Self-Replay Fine-Tuning (SRFT)**](https://openbmb.cn/en/blog/self-replay-fine-tuning), a fine-tuning approach that helps developers extend model capabilities at low cost while reducing forgetting of existing capabilities, making further customization easier. ## Get started

Model weights  ·  Inference  ·  Fine-tuning  ·  Live demo  ·  Local deployment  ·  API  ·  Cookbook

### On-Device Capability and Efficiency #### Smooth On-Device MoE Inference without compromising performance An MoE model can have far more total parameters than it activates for a single token, but its on-device storage requirements are not limited to those active parameters. Different tokens can select different experts at different layers, while device memory often cannot hold all expert weights. Without a latency constraint, weights can remain on SSD or other storage, be loaded as needed, and be released after computation. This makes large-model inference possible, but repeated loading stalls can make decoding too slow for real-time interaction. Another approach is to restrict the pool of available experts. For example, fixing an expert subset for an entire prompt can reduce loading frequency, but limits subsequent token-level routing to that subset, potentially excluding experts the model would otherwise select and reducing its capabilities. The central goal is therefore **smooth inference without compromising performance**: preserving model capability while delivering sufficient throughput under limited memory and bandwidth. MiniCPM-V 4.7 35B-A3B addresses this challenge through three complementary techniques: - [**Lookahead Expert Scheduling (LES)**](https://github.com/OpenBMB/llama.cpp-omni) uses cross-layer routing prediction to preload experts likely to be needed by the next layer. Among the experts selected by the actual router, it prioritizes those successfully prefetched and overlaps their computation with loading the remaining required experts. # Fish Audio Drama 3

**Fish Audio Drama 3** is Fish Audio's new-generation text-to-speech model, built for multi-character
scenes and long-form content. It supports multi-speaker generation, voice cloning and
natural-language control.

- **35B parameters, 3B active per token**: MoE text backbone with hybrid (full + linear) attention
- **Codebook-MTP audio decoder**: 10 codebooks decoded causally over the whole sequence
- **FP8 MoE experts** with the remaining weights in bf16
- **Speaker tags** `<|speaker:0|>` … `<|speaker:15|>` — one text can carry up to 16 characters
- **Long text** is chunked automatically and can be streamed per chunk

## Launch with SGLang Omni

Drama 3 runs on [SGLang-Omni](https://sgl-project.github.io/sglang-omni/) from launch day.  For installation, deployment, and streaming API examples, see the [Drama 3 Cookbook](https://sgl-project.github.io/sglang-omni/cookbook/fishaudio_drama3.html).

```bash
git clone https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-omni.git && cd sglang-omni
uv pip install --prerelease=allow -v -e ".[fishaudio]"
```

```bash
sgl-omni serve --model-path fishaudio/drama-3 --port 8000
```

## Example Usage

The reference clip the samples below clone, unmodified:

The reference, `en0` — a 3.9 s clip, the same `common_voice_en_10119832.wav` the cloning example above uses, with the transcript `We asked over twenty different people, and they all said it was his.`:

<audio controls>
  <source src="https://github.com/user-attachments/files/33393249/en0.wav" type="audio/wav">
</audio>

### Point tags

A plain `/v1/tts` request: one reference (`en0`), no history, and the tags written into the text at the position where the event should land.

```json
{
  "text": "[sighs] Fine. If we miss it, it's on you. [laughs] Well, maybe that's fair.",
  "references": [{"audio_path": "https://huggingface.co/datasets/zhaochenyang20/seed-tts-eval-mini/resolve/main/en/prompt-wavs/common_voice_en_10119832.wav", "text": "We asked over twenty different people, and they all said it was his."}]
}
```

<audio controls>
  <source src="https://github.com/user-attachments/files/33393205/A1_point_tags.wav" type="audio/wav">
</audio>


### Editing as continuation

Just send the previous VQ tokens and sent it as normal language models do.

```json
{
  "text": "The quarterly report is due on Thursday, so please finish it by noon.",
  "references": [{"audio_path": "https://huggingface.co/datasets/zhaochenyang20/seed-tts-eval-mini/resolve/main/en/prompt-wavs/common_voice_en_10119832.wav", "text": "We asked over twenty different people, and they all said it was his."}],
  "previous_takes": ["The quarterly report is due on Wednesday, so please finish it by noon."]
}
```

<audio controls>
  <source src="https://github.com/user-attachments/files/33393156/K1_edit_word_with_context.wav" type="audio/wav">
</audio>

A second edit chained onto the result of the first:

K5 chains a second edit: `by noon` becomes `by five`, with both earlier takes in the context.

```json
{
  "text": "The quarterly report is due on Thursday, so please finish it by five.",
  "references": [{"audio_path": "https://huggingface.co/datasets/zhaochenyang20/seed-tts-eval-mini/resolve/main/en/prompt-wavs/common_voice_en_10119832.wav", "text": "We asked over twenty different people, and they all said it was his."}],
  "previous_takes": [
    "The quarterly report is due on Wednesday, so please finish it by noon.",
    "The quarterly report is due on Thursday, so please finish it by noon."
  ]
}
```

<audio controls>
  <source src="https://github.com/user-attachments/files/33393164/K5_second_edit_chained.wav" type="audio/wav">
</audio>

## Production Serving

All numbers below were measured on NVIDIA H200 GPUs with streaming requests on Seed-TTS English prompts. Each request clones a voice from one pre-encoded reference (`vq_codes` with its transcript) and uses `temperature` 1.0, `top_p` 0.9, `top_k` 30 and `max_new_tokens` 500. Throughput counts generated acoustic frames per second. TTFA is the time to first audio. RTF is the time from sending a request to its last audio chunk, divided by the duration of the returned audio.

| Concurrency | Throughput (frames/s) | TTFA p50 | TTFA p95 | RTF (mean) |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 166.7 | 88.9 ms | 90.8 ms | 0.131 |
| 2 | 287.0 | 96.2 ms | 130.1 ms | 0.152 |
| 4 | 467.6 | 108.2 ms | 156.4 ms | 0.186 |
| 8 | 678.1 | 153.2 ms | 210.9 ms | 0.256 |
| 16 | 927.6 | 210.1 ms | 287.2 ms | 0.373 |
| 32 | 1,244.7 | 304.6 ms | 396.1 ms | 0.551 |
| 64 | 1,687.3 | 450.9 ms | 1,020.1 ms | 0.801 |

*Table 1. Drama 3 streaming performance on one H200. Each cell is the mean of four runs.*

A single stream gets its first audio in under 100 ms. At concurrency 16, audio is still generated about 2.7× faster than it plays back, and at concurrency 64 mean RTF stays at 0.80. ## Introduction **Qwen-Image-2.1-Turbo** is an accelerated checkpoint of [Qwen-Image-2.1](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen-Image-2.1) for text-to-image generation and image editing with **8 denoising steps**. It uses the same 7B visual generation architecture and loads directly with `QwenImage21Pipeline` in Diffusers. The checkpoint includes its recommended sampling schedule, so it is ready to use without manually configuring the scheduler. Generation uses CFG=1 by default, and prefix KV caching reuses the text and reference-image context across denoising steps. For more details, see the [GitHub repo](https://github.com/QwenLM/Qwen-Image-2.1) and [Qwen-Image-2.1 blog](https://qwen.ai/blog?id=qwen-image-2.1). ## Quick Start ### Installation Install a CUDA-compatible PyTorch build, then install the latest Diffusers source and the following dependencies: ```bash pip install git+https://github.com/huggingface/diffusers.git pip install "transformers>=5.17.0" accelerate pillow ``` This checkpoint requires Diffusers with support for pipeline-configured sampling sigmas, added in [PR #14950](https://github.com/huggingface/diffusers/pull/14950). ### Text-to-Image Load the checkpoint from Hugging Face: ```python import torch from diffusers import QwenImage21Pipeline pipe = QwenImage21Pipeline.from_pretrained( "Qwen/Qwen-Image-2.1-Turbo", dtype=torch.bfloat16, ).to("cuda") prompt = "A vertically oriented educational chemistry study poster fills the frame, designed like a hand-drawn classroom notes page with a clean white background, thick dark navy-blue outer border, and thin inner navy rectangular border lines. The overall aesthetic is colorful, high-contrast, and hand-lettered in a signature Topper style using marker and watercolor effects. At the top left, a small header in black handwriting reads \"Topper’s Notes\", accented by short decorative navy strokes radiating from it. Centered across the top is the main lesson heading in large stylized black-and-yellow bold lettering: \"Science – Chapter 1:\" followed below by the much larger title \"Chemical Reactions and Equations\". The title has energetic yellow highlighter strokes underneath and small sparkle doodles nearby. At the top right, inside a small outlined page-number box, the label reads \"Page X\". Below the header, a wide rounded rectangle framed in dark navy contains a pink brush-stroke highlight banner with the subheading \"IMPORTANT CHEMICAL EQUATION:\" in black. Inside the same equation panel, the reaction is written very large as \"Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu\". The symbol \"Fe\" is highlighted in bright orange with an underline, \"CuSO₄\" is vivid blue and underlined, \"FeSO₄\" is bright green and underlined, and \"Cu\" is metallic bronze and underlined. Beneath the left side of the equation is a lavender rounded label connected by a leader line to the iron component; it says \"Reactants\" and below it \"(before the reaction)\", with \"Reactants\" colored purple and underlined. Beneath the right side is a matching pale-green rounded label connected by a leader line to the products; it says \"Products\" and below it \"(after the reaction)\", with \"Products\" colored green and underlined. Along the lower part of this equation box are stylized ball-and-stick molecule models and atomic orbital drawings: a silver-gray sphere labeled \"Fe\" sits left of center, another cluster shows gray, red, and white spheres representing sulfate groups around blue and green atoms, and a copper-colored sphere appears near the right. Small atom-and-orbit icons sit along the bottom edge of the panel in blue, green, and brown outline styles. The middle portion is enclosed by a large dashed green rounded rectangle titled \"REACTIVITY CONCEPT\" in green uppercase letters with decorative rays. On the left side of this section, a stepped vertical reactivity-series ladder is drawn with alternating colored horizontal blocks. From top to bottom it lists \"K\", \"Na\", \"Ca\", \"Mg\", \"Al\", \"Zn\", \"Fe\" with a green oval callout reading \"(More reactive)\", then continues downward with \"Cu\", \"Ag\", \"Hg\", \"Pt\", \"Au\" with an orange oval callout reading \"(Less reactive)\". Each step is marked by a dark upward-pointing triangular arrow, showing decreasing reactivity downward. # Qwen-Image-2.1 Uncensored Quantized

GGUF, Safetensors, and MLX quantized formats of [Qwen/Qwen-Image-2.1](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen-Image-2.1) for local image generation using the original upstream base weights.

## Benchmark

![Qwen-Image-2.1 benchmark](assets/Qwen-Image-2.1-Benchmark.png)

| FP8 | [**qwen-image-2.1-UC-fp8.safetensors**](https://huggingface.co/abenzerps/Qwen-Image-2.1-Uncensored-Quantized/blob/main/qwen-image-2.1-UC-fp8.safetensors) | 6.63 GB |

Use the model with [ComfyUI](https://github.com/comfyanonymous/ComfyUI) and [ComfyUI-GGUF](https://github.com/leejet/ComfyUI-GGUF).

All required companion files (GGUF transformer, text encoder, and VAE) are hosted directly in this repository.

### 1. Download & File Placement

Download the files and place them in their respective ComfyUI directories:

```text
ComfyUI/
└── models/
    ├── diffusion_models/
    │   └── qwen-image-2.1-UC-Q4_K_M.gguf      # Choose one GGUF quantization (Q4_K_M recommended) or .safetensors

        └── qwen_image_2.1_vae_bf16.safetensors

   cd ComfyUI/custom_nodes
   git clone https://github.com/leejet/ComfyUI-GGUF
   ```

With only 2B active parameters per token, each reasoning token is cheap. - **Efficient inference**: Runs up to 1.7× faster than comparable MoEs on-device, with 184 tok/s on an Apple M5 Max and up to 21K output tok/s on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU. # FLUX 3 Image Klein for ComfyUI

![Launch gallery](./launch-gallery.jpg)

FLUX 3 Image Klein is a 5.6B open weights model for text-to-image generation and image editing. It takes a prompt and up to 10 reference images and returns one image. Text-to-image, single-reference edits and multi-reference compositions run through the same model, with Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct as the text encoder.

The 5.6B parameter label refers to the image transformer; the text encoder is separate.

This repository holds the model files repackaged for [ComfyUI](https://github.com/comfyanonymous/ComfyUI): the distilled and base transformers in BF16, int8 and NVFP4, the text encoder in BF16 and int8, the prompt upsampler in BF16, int8 and w4a8, and the image autoencoder. The original model repositories are [FLUX 3 Image Klein](https://huggingface.co/black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein), [FLUX 3 Image Klein Base](https://huggingface.co/black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein-base) and [FLUX 3 Image Klein Prompt Upsampler](https://huggingface.co/black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein-pup).

Inference code, prompt upsampling and the bounding box format: [black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein](https://github.com/black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein) on GitHub.

**Do not use the model without a prompt upsampler.** FLUX 3 Image Klein takes full scene captions, for text-to-image, editing and layout with boxes alike; a short prompt sent as typed gives generic output. Use ours, the `qwen3.5_9b_flux3_prompt_upsampler_int8_convrot.safetensors` file in this repository with `enable_prompt_upsampler` on in the templates (see [Using with ComfyUI](#using-with-comfyui)), or any LLM you prefer with a system prompt that expands the request into one full scene caption ([`system_prompts.json`](https://huggingface.co/black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein-pup/blob/main/system_prompts.json) has ours).

| Checkpoint | Format | Steps | Guidance | Built for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Klein Base](https://huggingface.co/black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein-base) | undistilled, bfloat16 | 50 | 3.5 | fine-tuning, LoRA training, research |
| [Klein](https://huggingface.co/black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein) | distilled, bfloat16 | 16 | none | generation and editing, self-hosting; the checkpoint behind the BFL API |

## Key Features

1. Text-to-image, single-reference editing and multi-reference generation in one model.
2. Bounding boxes in the prompt. Place elements with boxes on a 0 to 1000 grid, then recolor, move, replace or remove them through the prompt. Boxes guide placement and scale; they do not constrain pixels to a hard mask.
3. Text rendering within generated images.
4. Released under the [FLUX Kommunity License](LICENSE.md). The license permits non-commercial use and provides a commercial-output exception for Qualifying Users, subject to its terms. See [License](#license) below.

## Files

Place the files in the following folders:

```
📂 ComfyUI/
└── 📂 models/
    ├── 📂 diffusion_models/
    │   ├── flux3-image-klein-base-bf16.safetensors
    │   ├── flux3-image-klein-base-int8-convrot.safetensors
    │   ├── flux3-image-klein-base-nvfp4.safetensors
    │   ├── flux3-image-klein-bf16.safetensors
    │   ├── flux3-image-klein-int8-convrot.safetensors
    │   └── flux3-image-klein-nvfp4.safetensors
    ├── 📂 text_encoders/
    │   ├── qwen3.5_9b_flux3_prompt_upsampler_bf16.safetensors
    │   ├── qwen3.5_9b_flux3_prompt_upsampler_int8_convrot.safetensors
    │   ├── qwen3.5_9b_flux3_prompt_upsampler_w4a8.safetensors
    │   ├── qwen3vl_4b_bf16.safetensors
    │   └── qwen3vl_4b_int8_convrot.safetensors
    └── 📂 vae/
        └── flux2-vae.safetensors
```

Files with `-base-` in the name are the base checkpoint; the others are the distilled checkpoint.

| File | Content | Size |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `diffusion_models/flux3-image-klein-bf16.safetensors` | Klein, distilled, BF16 | 11.1 GB |
| `diffusion_models/flux3-image-klein-int8-convrot.safetensors` | Klein, distilled, int8 | 5.8 GB |
| `diffusion_models/flux3-image-klein-nvfp4.safetensors` | Klein, distilled, NVFP4 | 5.3 GB |
| `diffusion_models/flux3-image-klein-base-bf16.safetensors` | Klein Base, BF16 | 11.1 GB |
| `diffusion_models/flux3-image-klein-base-int8-convrot.safetensors` | Klein Base, int8 | 5.8 GB |
| `diffusion_models/flux3-image-klein-base-nvfp4.safetensors` | Klein Base, NVFP4 | 5.3 GB |
| `text_encoders/qwen3vl_4b_bf16.safetensors` | Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct text encoder, BF16 | 8.9 GB |
| `text_encoders/qwen3vl_4b_int8_convrot.safetensors` | Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct text encoder, int8 | 4.9 GB |
| `text_encoders/qwen3.5_9b_flux3_prompt_upsampler_bf16.safetensors` | prompt upsampler, BF16 | 18.8 GB |

The BF16 transformer and the autoencoder are the same files as `model.safetensors` and `ae.safetensors` on the original repositories. The int8 files run on 8 GB GPUs such as the RTX 3070, and on GPUs without FP8 support (RTX 30 series and older). NVFP4 needs a Blackwell GPU.
